title: Introduce canary-safe request class with strict rate limits + priority controls
author: Marcus Reed
description:
Problem: We’re standing up the perf-regression canary and need a guarantee that canary traffic can’t meaningfully contend with customer queues (esp. during noisy fleet events). Relying on “best effort” low QPS in the runner isn’t sufficient because (a) retries can amplify, (b) multiple regions/instances will run concurrently, and (c) scheduler heuristics can accidentally treat the canary as normal traffic.

This PR introduces a new request class, `CANARY_SAFE`, with explicit admission control + priority behavior end-to-end:

- Strict rate limits (token bucket) enforced at the edge and re-checked at the runtime admission controller
- Hard caps on canary in-flight requests per (region, gpu_sku, model) slice to prevent queue growth
- Lowest scheduler priority + “no-preempt / no-borrow” semantics so canary cannot consume reserved customer capacity
- Clear metrics for dropped/throttled canary requests so we can detect misconfiguration without paging on customer SLOs

Scope / implementation details:
- New enum value `RequestClass::CANARY_SAFE` and plumbing through request context (gateway -> router -> runtime)
- Admission controller:
  - `canary_safe_max_in_flight` (default: 2 per runtime instance)
  - `canary_safe_rps` (default: 0.2) and `canary_safe_burst` (default: 2)
  - Requests that exceed rate limits fail fast with 429 + `x-redwood-retry-after-ms`
- Scheduler:
  - Assigns canary-safe to `Priority::LOWEST`
  - Explicitly disallows pulling from shared “burst” slots used by customer traffic
  - Adds queue stats: `scheduler_queue_depth{request_class=...}` (existing metric, now includes CANARY_SAFE)
- Safety guards:
  - Feature-flagged: `--enable_canary_safe_request_class` default OFF (will be enabled only in canary runner env)
  - If a request arrives marked `CANARY_SAFE` while the flag is off, we downgrade it to `BEST_EFFORT` and emit a counter (protects older clusters from unexpected behavior)

Illustrative snippet (admission controller):
```
if req.class == CANARY_SAFE {
  if !flags.enable_canary_safe_request_class {
    metrics.inc("canary_safe.downgraded");
    req.class = BEST_EFFORT;
  } else {
    if !token_bucket.allow(now) || in_flight >= cfg.max_in_flight {
      metrics.inc("canary_safe.rejected", reason);
      return Err(HttpError::TooManyRequests { retry_after_ms });
    }
  }
}
```

Observability:
- New counters:
  - `canary_safe_admitted_total{region, model}`
  - `canary_safe_rejected_total{region, model, reason}` where reason in {rate_limit, max_in_flight}
  - `canary_safe_downgraded_total{region}` (flag off)
- NOTE: No per-request-id labels; model label uses the existing normalized model key (same schema as other runtime metrics).

Testing:
- Unit tests for token bucket and max_in_flight behavior
- Integration test validating canary-safe never increases customer queue depth in a synthetic mixed-load scenario (uses the scheduler test harness)
- Backwards-compat coverage for downgrade path when flag is disabled

Rollout plan:
- Land behind flag (this PR)
- Enable only in perf-canary runner environment first (us-east, limited models)
- If we see canary_safe_rejected spikes, adjust runner pacing rather than increasing limits

Related:
- ENG-2843 (canary runner skeleton)
- ENG-2854 (scheduler pinning / variance reduction)

Notes:
- This PR does NOT change customer-facing request classes.
- This PR does NOT introduce a dedicated canary queue; instead we use strict admission + lowest priority in the existing scheduler (lower ops complexity while meeting the isolation requirement).
commits: runtime: add RequestClass::CANARY_SAFE and plumb through request context
gateway: enforce canary-safe token bucket + return 429 w/ retry-after header
scheduler: map CANARY_SAFE to lowest priority; disallow shared burst slot borrowing
metrics: add admitted/rejected/downgraded counters with normalized labels
tests: token bucket + in-flight cap + mixed-load scheduler harness coverage
docs: add config flags + guidance for perf-canary runner
review_conversation: Sofia Ivanova (review): Can you clarify the priority semantics? Specifically: does LOWEST still allow canary to occupy slots when customer queue is empty? That’s fine, but I want to ensure it cannot steal reserved capacity during burst. Also, please add an assertion in the scheduler path that CANARY_SAFE never uses borrowable slots.

Marcus Reed (author): Yep, intended behavior is: canary runs only when there’s slack, and never borrows from customer burst slots. I’ll add an explicit guard + a unit test in the scheduler harness to lock this in.

Sean Gallagher (review): From paging hygiene perspective: I’m okay with this approach, but we need to ensure canary failure modes are visible. Please add a dashboard-friendly metric for rejects, and make sure the 429 includes retry-after so the runner doesn’t spin. Also: rate limits should be per-region effective, not per-host, otherwise scaling runtime pods increases canary volume.

Marcus Reed (author): Added retry-after header + `canary_safe_rejected_total`. Re: per-host vs per-region: gateway limiter is per gateway instance, but we also have runtime-side max_in_flight to bound impact. I can add an optional Redis-backed shared limiter later, but for v1 we’re targeting small fixed canary runner concurrency. I updated the doc with the combined bound and added an alert suggestion to catch unexpected aggregate admits.

Allison Grant (review): Metric schema: model label is fine if it’s normalized, but please don’t include gpu_uuid / host_id anywhere. Also, do we really need reason label? Ensure it’s a small fixed set to avoid cardinality issues.
Marcus Reed (author): Agree. Reason label is a fixed enum {rate_limit, max_in_flight}. No host-level labels; using existing normalized model key.
Rafael Mendes (review): Operationally, how do we keep older clusters safe? If perf-canary accidentally sends CANARY_SAFE to a cluster without this code, what happens?
Marcus Reed (author): Good call—added downgrade behavior when flag is off (`canary_safe_downgraded_total`) so old clusters behave as BEST_EFFORT and we can spot it quickly.

Omar El-Sayed (review): Can you also set `source=perf-canary` to automatically map into CANARY_SAFE at the gateway? Otherwise the runner has to set the class explicitly and we’ll inevitably miss it in some clients.
Marcus Reed (author): Implemented: gateway maps `x-redwood-source: perf-canary` -> CANARY_SAFE (behind the same flag). Runner can still set it explicitly, but this reduces footguns.
Sofia Ivanova (review): Re-ran with the guard/test changes. Looks good. Approving.
Sean Gallagher (review): With the downgrade counter + retry-after + documentation updates, I’m okay. Approving with the note that we may revisit shared limiting if aggregate admits creep up.
release_notes: Internal: Added `CANARY_SAFE` request class (flagged) with strict admission control and lowest scheduler priority to isolate perf-canary traffic from customer queues.
